newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-GULLIT BRINGS GLAMOUR BACK TO CHELSEA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GULLIT BRINGS GLAMOUR BACK TO CHELSEA.

text.p: Although his plaster cast and crutches hardly cut a dash along Chelsea's fashionable King's Road, Ruud Gullit can look upon his cracked ankle as something of a blessing in disguise.

The former Dutch international, who has brought glamour back to Stamford Bridge, was finding it hard to combine playing with managing his eclectic side of high-profile foreigners and their competitive homegrown team mates.
"The good thing is I can focus on my work as a coach and trainer," Gullit said before watching his side's 4-1 win over Portsmouth in the quarter-finals of the F.A Cup last Sunday.

Since his appointment as player manager last summer after Glenn Hoddle left to take on the England job, Gullit's appearances on the pitch have been rare and usually as substitute. But, at 34, the former European and world footballer of the year, still has a commanding presence, marshalling the midfield, with strength, energy and enthusiasm.
That energy and enthusiasm will now be channelled into keeping his talented but somewhat temperamental side in line for a place in Europe next season, without his help on the pitch.
"I am not aiming to be back before the end of the season," he said, "Though it's very frustrating having to watch them training from a chair and not being able to run up and down." "

Like most top players -- and the Dutchman was once hailed by former Ireland manager, Jackie Charlton, as the complete modern footballer -- Gullit is no stranger to injury. After captaining tthe Netherlands to success in the 1988 European championship and helping AC Milan to victory in the European Cup in 1989 and 1990, he had a series of knee operations.

He returned between bouts of injury, to show fans at Milan and Sampdoria his prodigious talent but fell out with the Dutch international management, making his final appearance for his country in 1994. Hoddle brought him to Chelsea in 1995 and the southwest London club has since enjoyed a resurgence of optimism and popularity.

The atmosphere at Stamford Bridge resembles that of the late 60s and early 70s when dedicated followers of fashion strutted from the trendy boutiques of the King's road to the less salubrious end of the Fulham Road to cheer on the likes of Peter Osgood, Bobby Tambling and Charlie Cooke. That team's success culminated in the F.A. Cup in 1970 and the Cup Winners' Cup the following year.
Chelsea's seats, some of the most expensive in the country, are filled these days with a veritable Who's Who of the rich and the famous.

They come to watch what would have been unthinkable in the 60s: two Italian internationals in the shape of Gianfranco Zola and Roberto Di Matteo, Italy's former top striker Gianluca Vialli, Romanian international Dan Petrescu, Frank Leboeuf of France and, of course, Gullit.
Only someone with Gullit's European pedigree could have enticed such a lineup to London, thought the injection of television cash into the premier league helped.

Melding continental ball skills with the more physical talents of homegrown players is no easy task and while Chelsea have produced some of the most entertaining football in the league this season they are sticking to club tradition by proving less than consistent.
"I have to make them perform every week, in a certain way, the whole match," Gullit said. "They realise now they have to improve themsleves and focus on every game."
Gullit admits he, and his Italian imports, are bemused by the British obsession with the F.A.Cup.
"Some players think more of Cup games than the league and I as an outsider find it difficult to understand that," he said.
"For me, I was taught in Italy that the champions' league was the ultimate goal...then you have the chance to be the best team in the Europe," he said.

Currently eighth in the league, Chelsea have only an outside chance of qualifying for the European Cup, but if their continental flair can overcome a highly successful Wimbledon side in the Cup semifinals next month, they have a good chance of emulating the 1971 team and making it into the Cup Winners' Cup.
"I have to learn how important it is in England and I will go along with it," the Dutchman added good-humouredly.
Humour and a relaxed style are hallmarks of Gullit's fledgling managment career. Even in the tightest of games he rarely looks nervous or upset and he is constantly smiling.
"Every game I am tense," he said. "I just express myself in a different way. Other people run around and jump up and down."
He says he never shouts or gets excited in the dressing room. "If you want to make a point you make it clearly without a fuss. Anyway it looks silly when a foreigner tries to shout in English,"

Gullit, son of a Surinamese father and Dutch mother, hardly need worry about his English. He is more articulate than many of his domestic players and speaks four other languages. British televisoin used him as a pundit during the European championship last year.
It is a sign of changing times in the English game that Gullit has been welcomed so enthusiastically at a club where in the late 70s racism was rampant among fans.

Today they are happy to wear dreadlock wigs just as the supporters in Milan and Genoa before them in honour of a politically outspoken footballing idol, who dedicated his footballer of the year award 10 years ago to the imprisoned Nelson Mandela.
Of course they would like to see him back on the pitch, but Gullit is obviously finding excitement and challenge enough in coaching.
He says he has not given up playing and counts himself lucky that he has gone straight from playing to coaching without the terrible wrench of a ending an outstanding footballing career.
"This way the door is still a little bit open."
